**Finding submitted: `missing` (INSURANCE)**

**What I found.** The Agreement contains no insurance provision at all — a full-text search for "insurance" returned zero hits, and the section outline has no insurance heading anywhere in the miscellaneous article (§ 14) or elsewhere.

**Why it matters here.** IBM is squarely a data-touching hosting vendor:
- § 5.3 (Security) confirms IBM operates the e-business Hosting Environment and implements security features for it.
- § 14.12 (Risk of Loss) shows IBM holds Base Components, with Customer Components in its environment.
- § 14.18 (Data Protection) states IBM processes **personal information on Customer's behalf** as part of the Services.

That last point puts the gap at the playbook's walk-away line ("no insurance for a vendor that processes personal data"), so this is not a waivable omission despite the rule's low severity.

**Redline.** Inserted a new § 14.12A "Insurance" immediately after the existing risk-allocation paragraph — the most natural anchor, since it sits with the other risk provisions and avoids renumbering §§ 14.13–14.20. Coverage is at the preferred level: CGL USD 1M per occurrence / 2M aggregate, E&O USD 2M, cyber USD 5M (justified by the § 14.18 personal-data processing), statutory workers' compensation, certificates on request, running through the term plus one year. Validated via `propose_redline` (ok:true) and aligned to the `seed-insurance` precedent.

**Negotiation note.** The comment flags the fallback (E&O USD 1M / cyber USD 2M) up front. Practically, IBM carries coverage well in excess of these limits, so the likely friction is procedural — IBM often resists contractual certificate-delivery obligations and prefers pointing to its corporate insurance program rather than accepting per-contract limits. If they push back, the certificates-on-request sentence is the cheaper concession to trade than the cyber limit.
